Don Menza and Sam Noto

Saxophonist Don Menza was born in Buffalo, NY on April 22, 1936. He attended SUNY Fredonia, New York but left in 1962 to join the Maynard Ferguson Big Band. After a short stint with Stan Kenton he worked in Germany for most of the mid-60s. Don joined the Buddy Rich Big Band in 1967 and became known for impressive solo on “Channel One Suite.” He became in integral player and arranger for Louie Bellson’s jazz orchestras and has returned to Europe numerous times in the ‘80s and ‘90s.

Sam Noto is also a native of Buffalo, born on April 17, 1930. He has played in the trumpet sections of the Stan Kenton, Count Basie and Louie Bellson Big Bands and led a bop based quintet with saxophonist Joe Romano. Sam has spent a good deal of his career in Toronto and has recorded numerous records with Rob McConnell’s Boss Brass. He can be heard on the Xanadu label and his sidemen include Blue Mitchell, Al Cohn and Dexter Gordon.
Don Menza and Sam Noto frequently perform together in Central New York jazz venues. They were interviewed at Hamilton College on January 28,1997 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive, and we don’t often think of the area of Upstate New York as a hotbed of jazz, but a great deal of jazz musicians have come out of Upstate New York and we have two of the finest here today — Don Menza, saxophonist, and Sam Noto, trumpet. Welcome to Hamilton.
Thank you.
Thank you.
You guys have shared some common experiences, you’re both from Buffalo, is that right?
Yeah.
When you were growing up in Buffalo, what was their jazz scene that helped spawn your interest in this kind of music?

Well, just for the archive, Sam is older than me, and by the time I was starting to get into music and starting to play, Sam was already on the scene, and I wasn’t old enough to get into a lot of clubs, and he was just past the age limit so I used to hear him play like at the — the first time I saw him really was at The Flamingo on Delaware Avenue, Delaware and Tupper — Chippewa. And I remember seeing him and Larry Covelli, also another great saxophonist from — jazz saxophone player from Buffalo, New York. And yeah there was a jazz scene. And there were a lot of people around. In those days there were two different unions, there was a black musician’s union and a white musician’s union, and unfortunately they merged, which became the demise of the black musician’s union. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

But it was a place to go play. Sunday afternoon jazz sessions, I mean sessions where you could play and you used to have to go in and almost sign up backstage and get in line and wait to play. And everybody was very — I mean so far as I was concerned — everybody was very encouraging to help me play and learn how to play, and a lot of great names — the Hackney brothers that played with, they both played with Dizzy didn’t they?
Yeah.
Wade Legge, Elvin Shepherd — I mean there were a lot of people there. Georgie Clark, saxophone player, and Otis Sutton.
When you say that unfortunately the unions merged —
Well I think that, I’m in the executive board of the local now.
No, we don’t want to get political about this now. I mean I was joking about it.
I’m interested in the scene between black and white musicians at that time, and —
It was healthier back then.
It was healthier then than it is now.

Now the blacks don’t want to stay in to the union. They feel that they don’t get enough. But the union doesn’t get you work, it’s just an organization that in case you’re in trouble and nobody pays you —

It was a protective society and a collection agency. And it isn’t like the AF of L or CIO or — the musician’s union was sort of a gathering of people that wanted to form some kind of common bond and be able to like have somebody protect them against club owners that weren’t going to pay them, or minimum wage scale. If you go back and look at the beginning of it it’s rather strange.
But when you got called for a particular kind of gig at that time, was it a mixture of players?

Oh yeah, oh sure. It was very healthy at the time in Buffalo. We all thought of course things aren’t happening, but back in those days they really were happening. It was like Miles and all of these bands, Dizzy, they were all coming to Buffalo. There was a venue for them there.
And more than one.

Oh yeah. There was a lot of places that really had top-notch, world-class musicians you know. And it was healthier in town. There was a lot of local things happening you know, and much healthier than it is now, although it’s picking up again in Buffalo. On the same street we mentioned, Chippewa, it’s like a rejuvenation. All the college people have discovered that area, and they’re all coming in and digging the music and hanging out and whatever they do you know. But it’s just coming back. In fact Don and I are playing there Friday night at this club right on Chippewa. And it’ll be mobbed. Of course they love Don in Buffalo. Me? I don’t know. © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

He does all right. We’ve heard a lot of different stories about how musicians actually learned the craft of jazz. Some of them that were born in the 20s mostly learned it on the road. Was this something that you guys — how did you learn your craft?

Well by doing it really. I mean you can go and learn all the tunes and the changes and all of that but unless you’re out there doing it — you do sessions all over the place. Free. You play free, but you were learning. And under the right guidance and with a lot of great players, and they would help. And that’s the way I learned, just by doing it. It probably was the same for you.

Absolutely. There were no schools. Academia still really hasn’t accepted jazz as a quote art form, and they really don’t know how to deal with teaching it. I mean there are so many, scores of different approaches to it. And some of them work, some of them don’t. I find the shortcoming — or backtracking — when I learned to play it was learn from records, I had to listen and then I started to copy, I started to— people say well if you think he plays good you ought to listen to this other guy play, and it was always it was a 79¢, 89¢, 99¢ for a ten inch 78 RPM and go out, wear it out and go out and buy another one until you got the solo down.
He’s not as young as he may sound.
That’s right. 78s.
Well, slightly younger than Sam. And not much. But in those days, three years was a lot. Or four or five years was a great deal. If you’re 15 and somebody else is 20, that’s a big span there.
It gets closer as you get older.
Right.

And by the time I had really started to get to the point where I felt I had some technical and musical prowess, Sam was already out on the road in Stan Kenton’s band and by the time he came back I was in the Army and then I came back again and he was gone, and then he came back to Buffalo and that’s when it all started.
But you had an interesting anecdote about your college experience and the practice room?
Oh, at Fredonia.
Yeah.

I went to, I never did graduate from Fredonia. I went there for three semesters, and two of which were separated by a short tour on the road, and then I went back to school, and while I was at school, I remember the signs on the practice room walls and doors — ‘NO JAZZ PLAYING’ and if they caught you, you were suspended.
A felony. Dixieland is a misdemeanor.
A major infraction. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

And it’s strange. I wanted to go back to school, and I mean it was two weeks before final exams, and I got a call from Maynard Ferguson. I didn’t even say goodbye. The next night I played my first note at Birdland.
No kidding.
I mean I just packed up my 55 VW with a cloth sunroof and the idiot stick directionals on the side, jumped in the car and drove to New York.
No question, right?

There was no question in my mind. Well I was sort of misled. I didn’t have enough money to go to one of the bigger universities. I didn’t want to go to North Texas State, for some reason I didn’t want to be that far from the east, from New York. I’m a New Yorker and I’m not particularly thrilled about the fact that I moved to California. It was very good to me but getting to New York and being in the thick of it — feeling all of those jazz players around you, there was so much history there man, I couldn’t wait to get there. But it was a major infraction. And the jazz players were on the Dean’s List. I mean the “Black List.” So really, and I’m not trying to belittle them, they didn’t understand what it was. They didn’t understand who we were and the creative part of it. And when I wanted to go back to school, they turned me down. They felt I was going to be a bad influence on the kids there. A short eight or ten years ago, maybe ten years ago, I got an honorary, not really a degree but a special commendation from the Alumni Association. Dr. Jewett is the man — remember Jewett Hall? He invented the orthopedic pin. They gave him a special honorarium. He went to Fredonia. There was another woman who was on the State Supreme Court. And she got an honorarium, not an honorarium but an honorary certificate or whatever it is, they honored us, and me. And I was bewildered. I said I never graduated from Fredonia.
“You wouldn’t even let me back in and now—”

And here comes, and when they called, I said, “Who is this?” And I thought it was some sort of a put on. But I went there and I very graciously received it, with a great deal of thanks, and everybody went up and gave ten, fifteen minute speeches, and I got up in front of them and I had a drink of water and I looked at them and I held it up and I said, “I just want you to know how thrilled I am about this, and it’s not for what I’ve already done. I promise you it’s going to be for what I’m going to do.”
I think you’re making good on that. Applause please.

And I do. I get out there and I’m very energetic and I give a thousand and one percent to clinics and symposiums and master classes that I give. I mean there’s not anything that I can’t help them with. And so be it. And if I can help spread not just jazz music but music in general — I’m a classical music fanatic — I would give up every note I’ve ever played © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
or written, if I could just once sing the first act of La Boehme in the style of Jussi Bjorling or Pavarotti.
Well you can’t. I’m afraid you have too many good things on record. You can’t give them up.

I would. I’d give it all up if God came down right now and touched me on the shoulder and put that tenor voice up here where it belongs you know, in that nasal passage, in a minute it would be over. No question.

He has influenced my wife because my wife used to listen to jazz records. Now I walk in the house and there’s like Luciano Pavarotti on. He gave her the records. It’s constant. I mean I love it you know, but it’s constant and she used to be a jazz freak, you know, loved jazz.
Well I guess, as Ellington said, “There’s good music and bad music.” Did he say that? He said a lot of things. It sounds like something he might have said.
Yeah, I think he did say it, yeah.
Sam, how did the thing with Kenton come about?

That was another strange story. I mean a bus had an accident on the Pennsylvania Turnpike coming to Buffalo to perform. And when they got to Buffalo, Conte Candoli and a few other brass players had hit the seat in front you know, and they wiped their chops out. And Conte’s wife was pregnant and she cracked her back, her vertebra, and so he had to leave the band. When they got to Buffalo they needed two trumpet players, so I got the call because I could play high notes. They called the union, you know, said, “You got somebody that can play high?” “Well I mean he gets high, but I don’t know.” Georgie Hobni, you know a black trumpet player in town, we played on the concert that night, and Buddy Childers was the first trumpet player, and we had a little rehearsal in the basement of the theater and then Stan came up and asked, “How’d he do?” He said, “Well he read the chart and everything’s fine.” So he says, “You want to go on the road for a few weeks until Conte comes back?” I said, “Sure.” So I went out and Conte decided not to come back and called Stan and said he was going to stay in California. So that’s how I stayed on the band. It’s a weird way to get on the band, but you know, that’s the way it happened.
Stranger things than that have happened.
How does Kenton fit into the jazz history, as far as you guys are concerned?

Well I mean I liked the man, he was a great man. I thought he treated people right. But I wouldn’t say he was a jazz musician. He just liked anything that was progressive and interesting. And as you can tell from his music, there was some very interesting things played but they were nowhere near jazz, like “City of Glass” and all of these things were really far out for the time you know. And as close as he got to jazz was in ‘55 the band © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

we had in 1955 where Bill Holman was writing. and then it started to lean towards the swing/ jazz thing and they had great soloists — Charlie Mariano, Lenny Niehaus, Frank Rosolino and Carl Fontana and there was a lot of good soloists on the band. And then the band leaned a little bit more toward jazz. But actually, Stan wasn’t really a jazz kind of person or musician. He just wanted interesting music. And it leaned toward jazz.

Yeah. He was an organizer and he presented and provided a vehicle for the players and the arrangers. He knew how to find the right arrangers for his music. The Bill Holmans, the Gerry Mulligans, the Bill Russos, Bill, I mean what’s his name, Johnny—
Richards, the “Cuban Fire” album, which is a collector’s item.
A lot of great writers.
It didn’t necessarily have to swing for Stan.
You know what? And he did present, as a front man it was priceless. He was that Toscannini out in front of a jazz orchestra.
He was a great front man.

Yeah, I mean he’d walk, he was like six foot seven, he walked out on stage, and I mean but he gave you that look when he walked out on stage, like he had, I mean he’d spread his arms and he’d cover the front of the orchestra.

I’ll tell you a story about the swinging thing. This was in the ‘55 band, that was about the swingingest band that I ever was on with Kenton, I was with them for seven years. It was Al Porcino, and you know, really some swing players. We were in New York, we had a night off, so Al Porcino, who’s got that voice, I don’t know if you know who he is, but anyway, he said, “Count Basie’s band is down at Birdland. I think everyone should go down and listen to Count Basie.” So we all did, but not because he said it, but we wanted to hear him anyway you know. And Basie’s band was really hot at that time. And Stan Kenton was in the audience too. I saw him across the room and the whole thing in Birdland. So the next day we get on the bus now, we’re leaving New York and we’re going somewhere, I don’t know, to the next gig, and Al says, “Stan! I saw you at Birdland last night. How did you like Count Basie’s band?” And Stan says, “Oh it was great,” he says, “but all they do is swing.” And the whole bus cracked up, man, the whole bus cracked up. But we know what he meant, that wasn’t, that was just the way he thinks about it. He thinks more like in structures and you know—
Orchestration.
Colors.
You know, yeah. But the way he said it.

And it’s funny, he used to put down some classical music and operas and everything, and yet his concept had to do with that, had to do with that staging, that kind of presentation. His jazz concept. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
I don’t remember him putting that down—
Oh, yeah.
The only thing I remember him putting down was country-western.

Oh no, he talked about opera and all that, he hated it man. Yeah. And yet it had a lot to do with, his concept was very much based on that classical sort of structure. But he was a sweetheart. I know I worked with the band a short time and I mean a very short time, I had left Maynard’s band to go with Stan Kenton, and the second night on the band I gave my notice. It didn’t swing.
It was the music, right?

Yes. And after Maynard’s band it was such a letdown for me, that I called Maynard, I tried to get my job back and Maynard was furious with me for leaving. And Stan was very sweet. He says, “I understand perfectly.” And I didn’t tell him it ain’t swinging, I said, “This isn’t what I wanted to do.” And I told him I said, “I have the greatest deal of respect for you,” and we remained friends to the day he died.
It’s also interesting that he left, from what I read, he left instructions that he did not want a ghost band.
He did not want a ghost band. And it’s happening all over the world.

Well they call them “tributes” though. He willed his whole library to North Texas State. So that’s where all the music is. But there are copies all over the place now, just run it through the machine.
Well his music was pretty popular with the college bands.
Well sure.
It was popular then but I mean his music was popular. It was a big time band in the late ‘40s, early ‘50s, it was huge.

Well the band, when I joined it was an all-star band. It was Lee Konitz, Zoot Sims and all those people were on that band. And that was — Conte, and then that was close to a swinging band also, because those were all pretty heavy jazz players. Frank Rosolino was on the band.
While we’re talking about great arrangers, you guys have written a great deal of music yourself, and was it a self-taught thing, or did you — from listening again and trying things out?

Well he’s into the writing now maybe more than I am. I was in Vegas in house bands, and I got a little bored with that so I started studying with one of the trumpet players, Wes Hensel, who was on the band, as far as arranging you know. And he gave me pointers and that, so I wrote some charts. But Don is really into the writing, and I don’t write as much as I should really, anymore.
You wrote some things for Rob McConnell, didn’t you? © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

No, I played on a couple. No I’ve never written. I’ve written a bunch of things that I’ve played in Buffalo with a local band, you know, we put a concert on. But I’ve never — Louie Bellson played one of my charts in his big band, called “A Couple of Dozen,” which is based on a row you know.
A tone row?
A tone row, yeah.
Not a Monk Rowe.
Not a Monk Rowe. You don’t want to base a tune on me. That was good.

I forgot.. I made a pun and I didn’t know it. MR. Well, Don, I think that there’s probably a significant number of saxophone players in this country who have a kind of a love-hate relationship with you.

It’s cool. As long as they — it doesn’t matter. You know the saxophone parts, it’s nothing, everything that I’ve written I’ve played. It’s all based on my small group concept, all my big band charts. Everything. It’s a mood that I’ve experienced on the bandstand and I’ve translated it to the big band, you know, to be able to organize it in that sense. I started writing in Buffalo a long time ago. I was always very inquisitive. I wanted to know how does he get that sound, how does he make that, how does he do this. There were, the early arrangers, early on were Bill Holman, I loved that linear writing that he did; Oliver Nelson, Gil Evans, and I can’t think of any arrangers or writers that haven’t touched me one way or another, and I finally came up with some sort of a concept. The classical music thing really got to me because then I wanted to know how do I orchestrate, how do I get this sound, how do I get that kind of sound from doubling. I went to the scores, I learned string writing from all the operas, from all the classical writers. There is so much out there, and I have this insatiable appetite to try and do it all.
He’s a workaholic is what he is.

Not really. I mean I do have my moments away from music. Sometimes I even abuse the fact that I should be, I mean that I’m taking a little time off. I’m into model railroads and I forget about my practicing my horn suddenly and my writing takes a back seat. But these last few months I’ve been real busy at it. I just finished doing about six things for Orange Coast College, there is some things coming up. And the writing thing I never really studied, except with the best writers. I tried to copy things that I heard on records. And it’s getting easier and easier. Now when I hear something I recognize it. I can relate it to something I’ve seen on paper or something I did — oh it’s that but he added this so he did, and I never really went to school for arranging. There’s a trap in the schools that teach this, especially with the kids with the computers. They are a slave to that. They don’t try anything. They make the mistake, they hear it there, it doesn’t work, they change it and it’s gone. The computer remembers it, but they don’t. It’s a huge trap. And © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

a lot of the people that write with computers, it sounds that way. If they were going to pick up the saxophone or their flute or the trumpet or the piano and play it on the piano, they wouldn’t write that. On the computer it’s there, they do it very slowly, and then hand the part to a player and expect him to play it. And there’s not a breath for like 16 bars. Where do you breathe?
The computer doesn’t need to breathe.

I’m just going through this with a saxophone player who is very talented and a very talented writer, he’s going to be incredible. And he came in with a shout chorus. He’s got trumpets starting on a high B above the staff. There’s written notes, D, E, F. And he wanted to use a classical term that’s called motor rhythms, which Stravinsky used all the time. He’d get this one thing going, like [humms] from “Firebird,” and underneath it, [humms]. And he’s got these two different things happening [humms], and it’s like a motor rhythm, and the machine starts. And not every wheel turns the same number of — it’s that effect that you get. Well he’s got the trumpet player playing [humms]—
Wiping the poor guy out.

I says, “When is he going to breathe?” You’ve got to write — I says, “You wouldn’t write that if you were playing it on your flute or your piccolo or your tenor. You realize I have to take the horn out of my mouth and breathe?” That’s the trap.

I think the space in music is just as important as the notes. You know you get a person like, an individualist and an innovator like Miles Davis, I mean he played one note and the beat’s going on, and he waited, and made you hear a bunch of other notes.
You would lean forward waiting for the next — trying to guess where he was going to put it.
Space is important then, you know?
And you played with another master of that, with Count Basie, right?

Yeah, well that’s another story. You know when I first got on the band I thought I was sticking out like a sore thumb, because the band was in its groove and relaxed, and some of the sections played in different time areas than the other sections, until the ensemble came, and then it just took off. And at first I mean I was have a little problem, you know, playing with that much relaxation with intensity. It’s like a relaxed intensity that you had to get, you know. Because it was after a week or so and I started to feel that thing, and it was quite a treat for me. I mean I played in one of the better Basie bands too.
That was in the ‘60s?

I was on two tours I made with Basie. ‘64 and ‘65 I think it was. Great man. I loved him, man, Basie. He never wasted any words, and just the way he played, just the way he was you know. If he liked you man he liked you. And he seemed to like me for some reason. We got along great. I thought he was a great musician too. He never got in the way. I © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
used to play solos on “April in Paris” and all of that stuff and he hit the chord just when you needed it, man, never overplayed.
Did you feel like, I mean in listening to you play last night, it sounded to me like Dizzy Gillespie listened to you.

I don’t know about that. Dizzy was a good friend of mine. Then when I joined Kenton’s band, Dizzy was on that tour, it was a big package tour, and Charlie Parker was also. So I got to hear these guys for three months, every night. So I was hanging around with Dizzy. And there’s a lot of Dizzy in me. He was one of my first influences. And then of course then Miles and Clifford and Fats Navarro was a big influence. But you know it’s nice for you to say but it doesn’t work that way.
Well, in playing with Basie, did you have to alter your style some to fit that, or did it just seem to work?

Not my style, it was just where the time was you know. Because we’d usually play up on the time, and that band played right on the time, sometimes a little back, so that was a little bit of an adjustment. But style, no, I played that Thad Jones chair, which was the modern kind of trumpet, and then Joe Newman played the other trumpet chair, which was more traditional. But Joe wasn’t on the band when I was, it was Albert Aarons, who was also a fine lyrical player, a beautiful player. I know Don knows him too. And it was great, I mean it was a great experience.
And you both have been with Louie Bellson on and off — Don for quite a while, right?

My stints were Stan Kenton — I mean in the beginning it was Al Boletto with a band out of New Orleans, and then Maynard Ferguson, Stan Kenton, and then the European thing with the Max Greger Big Band in Munich; and then coming back I went with Buddy Rich and then Louie Bellson and of course Henry Mancini, I worked with Henry for like almost 30 years. But I have to say in all the band leaders that I worked for, Buddy was the one. It’s a great shame I didn’t get to work with Basie. I talked with Basie a couple of times. He heard me play with Louie and he said, “I’d like you to play with the band sometime,” and my heart started beating. I would have loved to have gone on that band and played with that band. And it’s after the fact now. I don’t want to do it with the ghost band, I wouldn’t consider it. But to have done it when Basie was there, and been around him, and been able to like have hands on with all the history, yeah, that would have been a thrill. Because my likes lean towards that kind of big band, and that kind of swing, that kind of energy. I loved it. But getting back to it evolving, because like this has to be documented, Buddy Rich was the only real band leader I ever worked for. He told you the truth, mediocrity did not exist in his vocabulary. He was very hard on people and he expected them to give as much as he did in the band. But if something went wrong with the band, I mean if something happened, if there was any kind of scene, he pushed © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

everybody out of the way and he’d say, “You deal with me, this is my band.” And some of the leaders, and they were all very good, they’d back up and, “It’s your problem, you deal with it, you got it.” Buddy was incredible. He knew exactly what he wanted out of a piece of music, and he’d sit out front, he didn’t read — he had a lot of insecurities and he never gave you that impression by how he played. He had a lot of insecurities. He didn’t read any music. He didn’t know a lot about music, except he knew what was good and he knew what he liked. Nothing more, nothing less. And if you stood up to play and you stepped on it, you can be sure you’d never stand up and play again.
He was a hard man.
Well it’s good to hear — I mean you phrase it in a positive sense, that he was a—

Well the people that put him down are the people that were mediocre and that couldn’t play. And they hated him. I think it’s very simple. I mean you talk to Sweets Edison about Buddy and he says, “Oh man,” he gets like rekindled. You’d get ready to play, and Buddy’d be there and he’d be propelling you along, making it easier for you to play.
He had upstate people too. Joe Romano, Pat LaBarbera, Sal—
Sal Nistico played for him.
He loved those upstate players because there was a certain energy coming from the upstate people you know, right from Buffalo all the way down to New York.

And you know of course the great line from Buddy Rich when he was getting ready to go in for brain surgery. The anesthesiologist asked him, they were getting ready to wheel him in and they said, “Mr. Rich, is there anything you know of that you’re allergic to?” “Yeah,” he says, “country music.” On his death bed, he still had that kind of wry sense of humor. I have a video somebody just sent me, of Buddy Rich singing and dancing and playing. I mean it’s an hour long video of him on “The Ed Sullivan Show,” on this show, on that show, and he does a song and dance routine on “The Steve Allen Show,” and you should see him tap dance. I mean it’s nothing short of Gene Kelly and Fred Astaire. And he could improvise. He could get out there and do the whole thing.
I saw him in Batavia, New York, a long time ago.
He as an incredible talent.
At the Mancuso Theater. And he was dancing then.
It comes out of the Vaudeville training.
I may have been about 15, 16, I went down there with my older brother.
Well what a great thing for a drummer to start with.

And he could sing too. And on the tape, it’s like a song and dance and play routine. He comes out, he sings the song, he does a little tap dancing with a big arrangement that they had done for “The Steve Allen Show,” and then he sings some more, and then he suddenly winds up on drums and plays this tremendous shout chorus with the band and © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
then this tremendous solo, and then he stands up and he says, “That was nothing,” and for him it was.

Well you know I have to ask you about the recording you made of course. Even in the Grove Dictionary of Jazz it mentions the “Channel One Suite.” And it seems like there’s been certain times in jazz history where people have recorded things, you know Illinois Jacquet with I guess “Flyin’ Home” and Coleman Hawkins “Body and Soul,”
And Stan Getz “Early Autumn.”
And this particular recording, I’m interested in. Was that the only live recording done of that particular chart first of all?

No. There is a new recording that’s coming out on CD, it was live at Ronny Scott’s, it was Buddy Rich’s 50th birthday, and they’re re-issuing that. There’s also a beautiful concert hall where Benjamin Britten used to go and give his premier performances north of London called Maltings. Maltings on the Snapes. It’s like a swamp area, a bog—
A marsh?

Bogs and marshes, that’s what they are. But Maltings is a beautiful old concert hall, very, very experimental and a lot of flat surfaces reflecting and anyway, we did a television show there and it was recorded there. There is a studio recording of that same album of the “Mercy, Mercy” album that got shelved because we were in Buffalo, New York on my birthday in 1967 or 1968, and I remember Buddy telling me as I was playing more and more as the cadenzas got longer, he says, “Stretch out.” So in Buffalo, on my birthday, I really took it out and did a five minute cadenza in one breath, you know circular breathing and everything, and he went out front and dropped a cigarette and he said, “Oops, it’s one of those Don Menza roll your own.” This is at Kleinhan’s Music Hall, and I’m saying, oh no. And I was going to be the brunt of his jokes all night. He said, “Why didn’t you play like that on the record?” And I said, “Well you told me to play shorter.” I said, “But now that the band sounds so good, why don’t you do the record live?” He said, “Get your own band, kid,” you know, in front of 3,000 people. Well the wind up was two days later he gets on the bus and he says, “I want everyone to get your act together,” he says, “if we’re playing good now I want it even better. We’re going to do the album live at Caesar’s Palace in July.”
I was backstage when you guys did that. I was working across the street.
And we did it, and that’s the Gospel truth, that’s exactly how that — and Liberty or Pacific Jazz still has those tapes, the studio recordings of those tapes.

Well you’ve probably had people tell you this before, but you know my roommate and I just used to sit and listen to that piece over and over. And I was one of the unfortunate people that, of course our college band got the arrangement, and I had the part. So no © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
matter what you did, you could play really well, but everybody’s, “Well it sure wasn’t much like what Don played.”

You know I played it every night and I had a bag of tricks, and the bag kept getting bigger and bigger, and I had all the space in the world. He never told me, hey cut it short. Never once said that, no matter how long or how absurd or bizarre I got with what I played, he said, “You got it, that’s you.” And people said you have to see him on the drums in back of you — he’s got his foot up on the bass drum and he’s listening and looking at me, laughing you know, and like sometimes he’d egg me on — “yeah, that’s it, play, yeah,” he’d be screaming at me you know. And it was great. He gave me all the space in the world, he never once handcuffed me. I’ll tell you one night Joe Romano and I partied all day in New York. My daughter had just been born, this was October of ‘68. And we were working at The Riverboat. And Joe Romano and I walked in and I had a box of Havana cigars and we had been drinking all day. And we walked in and we did look a bit disheveled, you know, and I’m trying not to look at him. And at The Riverboat they had buttons on the floor right where I sat, and I had to press the button to turn the lights on and there was another button to step on to open the curtain. Well I could see him looking at Joe and Joe has this classic look about when he’s been partying too much, his hair down in front of his face. I didn’t have that luxury you know. And Joe is sitting there and he’s like warming up, and Buddy goes over and pulls his locks from his eyes and he says “uh huh,” and then he looks down at me and I’m fooling with my reed and I’m trying not to look at him, and of course with me my eyes are bright red and I’m trying not to look at him and he says, “Uh huh,” and he says, “okay,” he says, “Willowcrest,” which is a tenor-alto feature. And he used to play it fast [humms] in three [humms]. And he’d start playing and he’d scream, “Willowcrest” he says “Menza, get the lights, get the curtains.” Well I reach over and press this thing and all the lights go out, I pressed the wrong button. And then he says, “The lights, the lights!” And the lights are blinking on and off and I can’t get the curtain thing to work, and finally I stand up and I’m trying to find the button, and I’m looking at him and I’m like this, and I press the button, the lights go on, the curtains open, and I’m out in front of the band looking like this, and he cut the band off and he says, “This isn’t your band.” He comes out, closes the curtain, and he got on my case and Joe’s case. He says, “If you guys ever come on my bandstand like this again—” and then he started laughing. He says, “What have you been doing all day?” And the people are waiting for the concert. I said, “My daughter was born last night.” He says, “Oh, congratulations,” he says, “you didn’t bring me anything?” I says, “Yeah, I got you a cigar, I got a bottle of wine, I got a bottle of Cognac.” He says, “Give me these things.” He took the cigar and the bottle of Cognac and the curtain opens and he starts talking to the people about my daughter. © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
He was nuts man. Buddy was a natural guy. He did what he thought at that minute you know?

And that night is the night where my father-in-law and all my relatives from Long Island were in to The Riverboat to hear us play, and we went up to the bar and they wouldn’t let us stand at the bar. They says, “Uh huh, this isn’t for the band, you guys go down.” I says, “Don’t move.” I says, “Hey Buddy, they won’t let us — my family’s up there.” He says, “Who?” And he’s in the dressing room, slippers, this was after the first set, with a bathrobe, and he had his toupee off, and he says, “Who?” He walks straight through the club, up a big circular staircase that looked like “Gone With the Wind,” he says, “Where?” I says, “That guy over there.” “If you ever mess with my band again,” he says, “we’re out of here.” He says, “Guys, the drinks are on me.”
Oh, man that’s a great story.

Buddy was incredible. Yeah. You hear a lot of bad stories, a lot of people don’t like him. A lot of people, oh, hey, he was too arrogant and everything. He was a pussycat. He really was. And I’ll tell you he is sorely missed. That’s the kind of drummer that helps, he knows about playing the time, he knows about when to get exciting, you know maybe not my favorite way of playing, but I never heard anybody play any better.

There’s really a little bit of a negative story on that thing, it’s a joke, but this guy calls after Buddy had passed he called Buddy’s number and gets his wife or somebody, his daughter, answers the phone. And he says, “Is Buddy Rich there please?” Big lull you know. “Well Buddy passed on.” He says, “Oh, okay, I just wanted to make sure.”
I heard the same thing about Benny Goodman too.
Well sure, that’s a whole hour program, Benny Goodman.
Right. We’ve had some stories, but you know most musicians are fairly protective of one another.
Oh, yeah, most of the time.
I really enjoyed your perspective on him because—

It’s different from what you — I mean it’s unreal. When he was in the hospital I remember going to see him. I was on my way to Europe and Chuck Findley and I and Joe Romano to see him. We had a ride to the airport so we stopped at UCLA and this was just after his operation, and his left arm was gone, his left arm was totally paralyzed. We never saw him again. He had died while we were in Europe and his left arm was paralyzed. And he’d be laying there. And every time he’d yawn, his arm would raise. There was something in the nerve system and his arm would go up and then fall. And while we were there Jake Hanna came in. And Jake went over and gave him a hug and Buddy started crying, and he was a very humble man, really. And he said, “oh, Buddy, you’re going to be all right, you play more with one hand.” And he says, “No, Jake, look © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-
at this,” and he picked up his hand and dropped it, and Jake in his quick sense of — his sharp sense of humor looked at Buddy and he says, “Now you know how we feel when you play.”
That’s great. Sam, when you played in Vegas, that was a pretty happening town for music, live music.
You mean when I was living there, I lived there for seven years, and I just played in house bands and that you know. I wasn’t too happy there, it was just a one dimension town, show business.
Yeah, I mean there’s things that musicians do throughout their career that —
You make compromises.
You have to.
You do what you have to do.

I worked days, too. I drove cabs and worked in a car battery factory and the whole thing. It’s just whatever comes up. I mean I’m a family man, I come from a very strong type family so that’s the way I felt. I mean if I couldn’t do it playing the trumpet I had to do something to keep some bread coming in you know. So I mean I’ve done a lot of things. And that’s why I decided to move to Vegas. I was making $82.50 a week in a car battery factory, and that’s 5-1/2 days a week. So I figured well, you know, I could make more money by blowing the trumpet, even if it’s not the way I want to blow it. So I went to Vegas and got into house bands and making five hundred a week and everybody was happy except me. But we played though, we used to play in people’s houses after the gig. You know Roy Shane, he had a big—
I used to go up and see him, we used to go up and see him, we used to go and hang out for three days.
He had a big studio in his garage. He’d turn the tape on and we’d play all night. He must have tapes that —

My wife — it’s interesting, this was one of the first times I could really show her what was happening. She wanted to come with me and we drove up to Vegas and we went to see Sam, we saw a couple of different shows and everything, and I said, “You’re going to come up and you’re going to hang with us for three days, you’re going to see what we do.” Because anytime, you know, four o’clock in the morning, six o’clock sunrise, you’re walking in after leaving at like six o’clock the night before. “Where do you go? What do you do?”
They think it’s another woman.

I says, “You’re going to hang with us, you’re going to see.” Well after a day and a half she says, “Drop me off at the hotel. Do what you want.” She couldn’t believe it, the life of hanging out and playing. In those moments, more great choruses were lost forever, had © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

disappeared into air, at sessions at three o’clock in the morning in Harlem and at the jazzkellers in Germany or little roadside cafes where somebody felt like playing and took out the horn and went up and played with the rhythm section you know, on a Sunday afternoon. There used to be places in Buffalo where, I mean all over the world there were places where you could go and play and you could practice. Now you’d practice, but you’d go out and show your wares.
Couldn’t buy any groceries though.
And it was for the love of it. We learned to play for the love of it, not because we thought we were going to make a living on it.
You owned a club too, didn’t you?

Yeah, I had two actually. The first one was in the mid-60s it was a coffee house. I couldn’t get a booze license. That lasted about a year and it was great. People, we’d stay open until six in the morning, after the bars closed, they’d all line up and have steak and eggs at my place and hear music all night. Joe Romano and I had a group there, like for a whole year. But then the last venture was about ‘82, and I had the whole ball of wax then, the bar and the booze and the whole thing. But it was in a bad area, it was between the black and white line there and the whites were afraid to come and the blacks wouldn’t come because it was a white owner. So that place went down fast, real fast. That was all my money, too.
It was called The Renaissance?

Yeah. They were both called Renaissance. The first one was The Renaissance and the other one was The Renaissance Two. I had some good players, I had Chet Baker there and Al Cohn and David Schnitter come in and played with Pepper Adams. I had some good people there but nobody would come to hear them. They did come to hear Chet and they did come to hear Don, they disregarded whatever area it was from you know. So Chet Baker was there for three days and it was mobbed every night. I charged seven dollars at the door and people were complaining, you know? “Seven dollars, Sam!” I said, “Hey man, Chet Baker. How am I going to pay this guy?” The drinks were a buck seventy-five. I mean drinks though.
Real drinks.
Yeah.
Owning a club I think is a tough business.
It’s a hard row to go. People don’t have any idea. The organization of it alone, just booking somebody for one night a week, 52 weeks a year, is a full time job. Incredible.

I go both ends of the stick on that one. That’s why I feel for a guy like at Tiny’s you know, and any club owner. I know what it takes to pay the musicians and still try to come out with your head above water you know? © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
It’s interesting to think I guess in the ‘40s and when this kind of music was the popular music, that with all the bands touring and so forth, that it certainly has changed.

Well there’s still a big audience for this kind of music but everybody’s a little afraid to come out anymore. You know like they think the cops are going to be there busting them if they have a drink and that kind of thing. And they stay home, they play their records.

Life has changed drastically. I mean it used to be where the urban situation was centrally located. It was easy. There were a lot of people there, there was a certain amount of security, you didn’t have to worry about being bowled over by a bunch of thugs or by some gang members. I mean there was still problems but in any large city that’s going to happen. But there seemed to be a certain amount of safety or you felt secure going downtown. A lot of bright lights, everything was there. The theaters, the restaurants, the jazz clubs, the little bars. You seemed to know everybody. They’ve done away with that. If you want to go somewhere to hear music you have to drive clear across town to some dark little shopping plaza that’s closed except for this one thing, and park like a quarter of a mile away—
Or else you go to a concert hall. I think some of the things that ruined the whole club scene were the concert halls and the big money that these bands demanded.
It’s a big business.
Thousands and thousands of dollars you know.
Not to mention what they’re presenting as jazz in the concert halls.
Well it’s interesting because I’ve often wondered when even with guys like yourself, when you were learning jazz, did you think of it as an art form? Did you think of it as high art?
Absolutely.
You did.

Yes. It was a creative art form. And I don’t remember using those exact —. but there was a mystique about it and any time I got ready to ask a musician who I thought was accomplished at all, maybe not a jazz player, but when I asked him about the jazz players and how do you learn to do that, they didn’t know. He says, “Oh he just makes that up.”
Plays anything he wants.

Yeah. Anything he wants. A lot of wrong notes. He plays out of tune and that. And I didn’t hear that, what I felt was the spontaneity, the inventiveness of it and it was always exciting to hear three saxophones playing on the same horn, same mouthpiece, and they all sounded different. It just didn’t sound like twenty violin players sounding the same. And that isn’t quite true either, you know.

With me, I never thought of it as an art form or that, I just heard it and I said well this is what I want to do. And I thought if I got good enough at this, you know, I could possibly © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

make a living doing it, which was a big mistake you know. Even like the Charlie Parkers couldn’t make a living, who was, to me, one of the best or the best jazz player around ever. But I dug it. I mean there was some vital — something vital about it. It tells the whole story about life and I mean I just fell in love with it. And before that, I used to listen to Harry James as a great player and everything, but when the bebop thing came out, it changed my whole life you know? And I keep telling all these guys, man, I could have been another Harry James.
The timing was a little off then.

I think the thing about what Sam says, we agree on it a thousand percent. I think it was the unpredictability of the jazz players. I mean you could go there and you never knew what was going to happen. And this is what makes for — puts the vitality in the music.

I play in Toronto a lot you know, I have a group up there, and all college kids come to hear us now, and they’re really into it. The more we get into the music, the more they like it. I mean it’s really intriguing — improvisation is intriguing in every aspect of the word in every business. So when something happens like that man, it’s great, you know, the spontaneity of it and a quick, good idea, no matter what you’re doing, no matter what end of the business or spectrum.

And it’s funny, the whole world looks at jazz players and jazz music as a vital art form, as a very important art form of the last fifty or hundred years — not here. Now they’re just starting, sort of like coming around to it but not here. If Woody Herman had gone through his number like he did when he was dying and when the IRS was ready to wheel his bed out in the street and take his house from him, anywhere else in the world he’s a hero, he would have been a national hero. But not here. It’s rather sad.
I think that somebody bailed him out. I hate to mention his name because I can’t stand him.
Yeah, it’s okay.
Frank Sinatra bailed him out a little bit, helped him out you know.
Yeah he did.
I think he let everybody know it too.
Not one of my favorites.

Well I’ve always felt that sometimes we look on music that comes from somewhere else as being more worthwhile, having the exotic end of it, and something that’s home grown we sometimes take advantage of it. But I also think maybe when dancing, for whatever reason became separated from the music that that changed it somewhat. And sometimes it seems kind of odd to be listening —
They used to dance to jazz.
Right. © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
And like to the bebop. Even the bebop era, they had a special dance that they did. I mean not just a special dance, but it was a concept, and they improvised out there.

In the late ‘40s in Buffalo, there was a place on the east side called Amity Hall and there was a big poster out front, “Charlie Parker Quintet.” And it was a dance hall. And it was Charlie Parker, Kenny Dorham, and it was a great band. And they were playing, and people were dancing, I mean it was a dance. We were standing in the corner listening, people were listening, people were dancing. And I thought that was pretty healthy, at the time, you know I’m not a dancer you know so I don’t know exactly what people get out of dancing, they must get something out of it. But I thought it was healthy because no matter what tempo, they tried to dance. And Bird played some fast tempos you know, and Dorham blowing them away man, beautiful.
Well it does seem kind of odd sometimes to be listening to say the Count Basie Orchestra in the concert hall, and they’re just swinging and swinging. People almost should be dancing to this music.
They did.
Yeah, but now, it’s not presented in that fashion. I don’t know if it’s right or wrong.
I don’t know either.
In concert halls very often you get so far away from the music that you lose that communication, that line of communication.
I think you also get the musician who is trying to be on his best behavior, I think he loses something in that performance because he wants to be perfect—
He’s under a microscope, under a magnifying glass.

Everybody’s relaxing you know, and this guy may step out and do something really good, above his head for a minute, and then you’ll work off of that and learn something, see? But I think it gets more contrived as it’s presented in a concert way. But classical music is all on the paper. You know, save maybe a violinist doing a thing, you know, like a cadenza or whatever. But it’s there. You do that. And the beauty of that is to do that properly. But jazz is different. You do— when it comes naturally and spontaneously is the best part. But sometimes in a concert hall you may lose some of that.

Interesting concept. There’s a whole group of jazz players and a school of jazz players who believe: find a good solo and stay with it. And they play it the same way, they play the record version every night. Then there are the players who don’t, who play and every time they play they go looking for new things. And everybody has their thumbprint, they repeat little nuances that they do. But I would tend to lean toward that. A variation on the same theme. And where does the creativity end? I mean when you play the one solo and then you do it every time that way, then it’s not creative anymore. © Fillius Jazz Archive -20-

Well I got a kick out of last night when you guys were playing and you did “All the Things You Are,” which I’m almost always going to hear at a certain tempo, you know, most people are going to play it at a fairly uptempo, and you guys —
You never know what’s going to happen with he and I.
—were like way, way back with the tempo.
You never know what we’re going to play.

And it allows you to play, forces you to play a little different, and then you did the next tune, I can’t remember the tune, which is usually a ballad, and you did it up. I said what a great way to prod yourself into —
Well I think it’s interesting for the listener too, see now the reason you’re saying that, like it did, it rang something in your brain, right?

Pushed a button. That’s what the music is supposed to do. It’s not supposed to be just one way all the time. That’s what he’s talking about that same solo thing. I mean I don’t know how anybody can do that. I don’t remember what I played the last time anyway. What’s the point. Even with great classical players. I’ve heard Pavarotti say, “I’m an interpretive artist.” He’s taken this and I think that’s what put him over the edge as far as popularity is that he just doesn’t go out there and sing it like all the other great tenors that have come before him. There’s something just a little bit different about him. James Galway is that way. He considers himself an interpretive artist. He plays the same old Mozart which I hold with a great deal of reverence, he plays the same Mozart concertos that everybody else plays, but here comes this man playing it and he made it come alive. Again there’s a vitality in it. There’s an urgency in the music that I’ve heard a million times. It’s very interesting to hear people do that, take that printed page and why does it sound so much better than the guy who played it last time, who played it perfect? It’s that little edge, that little bit of interpretation where you take things and here comes my personality.
Well this has really been fascinating. You guys have given us some great stories. I didn’t get to ask you about your L.A. days too much, but you had—
L.A. is what it is, la la.
—you had a lot of studio work.

Oh, yeah. And I have to say one of the really great thrills of my life was working with Henry Mancini, and I sorely miss him. And he was exactly like his music. He made a big influence, a huge influence on me, like so far as my writing, arranging, seeing him in front of an orchestra. The great, great story from Mancini is when Pavarotti did his movie, I asked Hank, I said, and on his birth certificate it says Enrico, his real name was Enrico. I said, “Hank,” I said, “you going to do the movie?” He said, “Oh, no, they’re going to get a classical,” you know, well John Williams did it, he wrote the songs for the © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-

movie. Three years later, we’re celebrating, my wife and I are celebrating our twenty- fifth anniversary and we’re in San Francisco. We check into the hotel and here’s this little flowers and champagne and the whole thing. And Hank calls me and he said, “You going to come with me to rehearsal?” I said, “Well Rose is with me.” He says, “I know, bring her.” He said, “I’ve got to talk to you.” I said, “You want to talk to me?” I wonder what for? He calls me when he wants to talk to me. We get in the limo and he pops a — hands me a cigar, happy anniversary, we’re drinking and Rose loved him, he was great. And he says, “I just got a call from New York, they want me to write Pavarotti’s next album.” I said, “I told you.” Well I tried to find out where they were going to do it, and I wanted to go, I wanted to be there, I wanted to be part of it, to witness it. And they wound up doing it in Geneva, Switzerland because he was performing and he was singing Balla Maschera. [phone ringing] It’s not for me is it?
You’re late for a gig. We hope not.
Get me on it.
We supposed to be somewhere?

Anyway, the windup was he calls me as soon as he came back from the recording sessions and he says, or Rose says, “Don, it’s Hank.” I said, “Hank who?” She says, “Hank who?” She says, “The boss.” And I got on the phone I says, “Hey, how you doing, man?” He says, “Thank God I grew up in an Italian house.” I said, “Why?” He says, “I did all the right things with the music.” He said, “It was like I knew all of this all my life was coming to this.”
His heritage came out.
Oh, absolutely. And he understood it perfect. It was incredible.
He must have listened to Giuseppe Verdi now and then.

He and Pete Rugolo are great friends who wrote for, one of the arrangers who wrote for Stan Kenton in the early years, Pete Rugolo, David Rose and there’s somebody else and Mancini. They were all in Hawaii with their wives, like vacationing, in the early years. And Hank went into a fortune teller, I mean just off the street, the four of them. Everybody else went first and then Hank. And she says, “I see a great deal of success in your life,” she says, “and in your former life your name was Green.”
Which is Verdi, you know, which is Italian for Green. So we call him Joe Green.

Two weeks later, Hank was, and Hank told me this story, two weeks later he was in Los Angeles at Universal City and he was a ghost writer, and he was getting like B movies like “The Creature from the Black Lagoon” and all of that. And Blake Edwards was walking by him and he says, “Hank” he says, “I got a new series starting,” he said, “I’m going to call you next week.” He called him next week — “Mr. Lucky.” And the rest is history. © Fillius Jazz Archive -22-
Fascinating.
He said, “I don’t believe in any of that stuff.”
Well Monk, how are you putting up with us this long, man?
I’m just soaking it in. I love the stories.

And Hank, we’d get on an elevator and Hank was beautiful, we’d get on an elevator and you’d hear [sings “Moon River”] and you know and I’d try not to say anything, and there’s a bunch of people around us and we’re all standing there and nobody knows who Mancini is, and you know we’re all standing there and I sort of like chuckle, and I look at him, and he’d look over at me out the top of his glasses and he’d say, “Another beach house.” He was precious man.

Well, on behalf of Hamilton College, I want to thank you gentlemen for sharing your exploits and your insight into the music, so I hope you have a good trip to Europe, and you’re back to Toronto sometime soon?
Yeah, I’ll be up there, well we’re playing there Thursday, but I’m going up in May again playing up there for four or five days, whatever.
Well thanks so much.
Thank you, my pleasure.
Thank you for having us.
Okay. © Fillius Jazz Archive -23-
